title: Two right angles in one triangle?
hook: Put two square corners on one base. What would the third corner have to look like?

knows: a flat triangle's corners add to 180° (tear-the-corners)
doesNotKnow: proof by contradiction as a method: assume the thing and follow it until it breaks

misconception: "No triangle has two right angles" is a rule you are told, not something you can show. A tall enough triangle might manage it.
objective: The learner can explain that assuming a flat triangle has two right angles leaves 0° for the third corner, which they saw as the sides running parallel, so the assumption is false: proof by contradiction.

claims.text: The corners of a triangle on a flat page add to 180°, so two right angles (90° + 90°) would use all 180° and leave 0° for the third corner.
claims.source: Draw the parallel to the base through the top corner; alternate angles give the sum 180° (Euclid, Elements I.32). 180 − 90 − 90 = 0.

claims.text: With a right angle at one end of a base and angle B at the other, the sides meet tan(B) bases up and the top corner is 90° − B: at 89° that is 57.3 bases up with a 1° tip (stage readouts 'Sides meet' and 'Top corner').
claims.source: Right triangle: opposite / adjacent = tan B. node: Math.tan(89*Math.PI/180) = 57.29; tan 85° = 11.43; tan 60° = 1.73. The stage prints meet(B) = tan(B) with fmtH (2 decimals under 10, 1 decimal under 100) and 90 − B. The reveal quotes the largest B from 85° to 89° the learner set.

claims.text: On a flat page, two lines both at right angles to the same base are parallel and never meet (stage: at 90° the readout says 'never').
claims.source: If they met, the triangle formed would have corners summing to more than 180° once the top corner is counted, against c1 (Euclid, Elements I.27-28). The stage draws both sides vertical at B = 90° and meet(90) returns null.

claims.text: If an assumption leads to something impossible, the assumption is false; showing a statement this way is proof by contradiction.
claims.source: Definition of proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) in any introductory logic or proof text; no number to check.

claims.text: The lesson is set on a flat page: the stage caption says 'Flat page'. (On a sphere a triangle can have two or three right angles, which is why the condition is stated; the lesson does not claim anything about spheres.)
claims.source: Scope statement from the brief (company/domains/briefs/math.md #56, 'Not claimed'). The learner only sees 'Flat page' / 'On a flat page'.

recall.question: On a flat page, can a triangle have one right angle and one corner of 100°?
options: Yes, if it is tall enough
Yes, if its base is short enough
recall.why: Assume it could: 90° + 100° is already more than 180°, the most a flat triangle's corners can add to. The assumption breaks, so no such triangle exists.
